3.text: most part, of new animals just bought from strange herds, and the mutual

4.text: attachment of these reindeer was less strong than in an ordinary herd: so

5.text: Čêpaˊt lost a few animals almost every summer. One year, quite a large

6.text: group of reindeer, more than three hundred, strayed off and were lost. Then

7.text: news came from the Oloi River that the reindeer had gone to Eiˊheli, and

8.text: had been appropriated by him. After that, every time they met at the spring

9.text: fair, Čêpaˊt asked Eiˊheli about his reindeer, but Eiˊheli most stoutly denied

10.text: having any knowledge of them. In the year 1895, Čêpaˊt even talked about

11.text: his intention of robbing the camp of Eiˊheli on his return home. Then fol-

14.text: Theft among the Maritime Chukchee is less frequent than among the

15.text: Reindeer tribes, perhaps on account of the absence of valuable objects. I

16.text: know of some cases of robbery, however. One had already been mentioned.¹

17.text: It refers to the people of Quluˊči, who complained of the inhabitants of

18.text: Luᵋˊren. The latter robbed the dog-drivers of Quluˊči when they were returning

19.text: to their country from the Pacific shore with a load of foreign wares.

20.text: Another case refers to a Chukchee of Mariinsky Post, Qoplaˊnto by name.

21.text: This man, in the winter of 1898, met in the open country two young men

22.text: of the village Valqaˊʟên, who were going to Mariinsky Post with a supply of

23.text: brandy for trading-purposes. Qoplaˊnto joined them, spent a night with them

24.text: on the snow, bought some liquor of them with fur-skins he had with him,

25.text: and in the end robbed them of more of their brandy, and went away. They

26.text: were two, but, being in a strange land, they did not offer much resistance;

27.text: the more so, as Qoplaˊnto was the master of the front house of the Chuk-

28.text: chee settlement on the north shore of the Anadyr estuary, opposite the Rus-

29.text: sian post. When Qoplaˊnto was leaving, however, they said to him, “Now,

30.text: you too be careful not to come to our country. We shall take our chance

31.text: then.” In the winter of the year 1900, when I wanted to go to the northern

32.text: villages, Qoplaˊnto at first offered his assistance in transporting my load; but

33.text: when the time for departing drew near, he declared that he was afraid to visit

34.text: the village Valqaˊʟên on account of that affair; so he had to stay at home.

35.text: LAWS REGARDING PROPERTY. — I have already stated that with the Reindeer

36.text: Chukchee the paterfamilias is considered to be the owner and the master

37.text: of the herd, even though he be of extreme old age and infirm. I have noted

38.text: down some facts within my knowledge referring to this subject. On the

39.text: other hand, I was told by my Chukchee informants that when the son be-

40.text: comes full-grown and able to take care of the herd, the father, often of his

41.text: own free will, transmits to him the direction of the herd, and himself takes

42.text: the position of an assistant, even though he still be strong and able to work.
